item.title: Discovery and SAR Studies of Viral Processivity Factor 8 (PF-8) Inhibitors as Anti-Kaposi’s Sarcoma-Associated Herpesvirus (KSHV) Agents
item.description:
Abstract
Kaposi’s sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) causes several malignancies, while current antivirals targeting viral DNA polymerase provide limited clinical benefit. Here, we explored the viral processivity factor PF-8, an essential cofactor of the viral DNA polymerase, as an alternative antiviral target. Guided by similarities between PF-8 and the bacterial β-clamp (DnaN), we synthesized and evaluated 54 derivatives of a hit compound. Screening in reactivated KSHV-infected cells identified several inhibitors with low-micromolar antiviral activity. Selected compounds directly interacted with recombinant PF-8, as demonstrated by SPR and MST, and induced its thermal destabilization. STD NMR and docking studies provided insight into the binding epitope and putative binding mode. The most promising compounds, 1 and 38, inhibited viral DNA replication and reduced ORF45 protein expression. SAR analysis identified the 4-tert-butylbenzenesulfonamide and N-benzylpiperazine motifs as important for activity. These results support the investigation of PF-8 as an antiviral target and provide starting points for further optimization.

item.title: Fold-Stabilized Zn(II) Metallohelices Inhibit mTOR Signaling and Modulate the Tumor Microenvironment in Intrahepatic Cholangiocarcinoma
item.description:
Abstract
Water-stabilized metallohelices based on labile metal ions remain rare because of hydrolytic instability. Here, we report the design and synthesis of a unique class of optically pure, water-soluble, glycosylated Zn(II) metallohelix diastereomers that exhibit exceptional hydrolytic stability and potent, stereochemistry-dependent antiproliferative activity against intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC). In an orthotopic, AKT/YAP-driven ICC mouse model, treatment with the lead compound Λ-7a produced significant tumor growth inhibition. Mechanistic studies revealed that treatment with Λ-7a induced cell cycle arrest and apoptosis, accompanied by suppression of PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway signaling and reduced phosphorylation of downstream effectors. In addition, Λ-7a treatment was associated with reduced vascular and stromal marker staining and increased CD8+ T-cell and macrophage markers within the tumor microenvironment. Together, these results establish fold-stabilized Zn(II) metallohelices as a new class of metallodrugs exhibiting potent anti-ICC activity, suppression of AKT/mTOR pathway signaling, and treatment-associated changes in vascular, stromal, and immune-cell markers within the tumor microenvironment.

item.title: Discovery of Potent Orally Active Plasmodium N -Myristoyltransferase Inhibitors Using Fragment-Linking Approaches
item.description:
Abstract
N-Myristoyltransferase (NMT) is an essential eukaryotic enzyme and an attractive potential drug target for parasitic infections such as malaria and leishmaniasis. Co-crystallisation of a high-throughput screening hit with P. vivax NMT identified a novel binding mode, and cooperative binding experiments with fragments identified synergistic improvements in potency and opportunities for fragment-linking. Optimisation of the torsional angle of fragment linkage through phenolic ether enabled the desired activity spectrum and selectivity profile, and examples were progressed to a mouse malaria model, resulting in the selection of IMP-1002 for further evaluation. This early lead compound was efficacious after oral administration in a SCID mouse model and is highly active against both blood- and liver-stage forms of the parasite. Finally, we discovered that highly potent human NMT inhibitors, including IMP-1088, could be generated by introducing an additional fluorine atom to further tune the torsion angle.

item.title: A Pt(IV)-Cluster-Nanobomb for Concurrent Activation of Triple Programmed Cell Death Pathways: A New Effective Method to Overcome Cisplatin Resistance
item.description:
Abstract
Activation of single programmed cell death (PCD) pathway frequently contributes to the development of cisplatin (CP)-resistance. Herein, we designed and synthesized a series of carrier-free Pt(IV) nano-prodrugs designated CSPNPs (6aNPs−6dNPs). These prodrugs integrate three functional components into a single entity: CP as the core PCD-initiator; disulfide-cinnamic acid (CA) derivatives as amplifiers; and hydrophobic chains for self-assembly. Enriched in tumors via enhanced permeability and retention effect, CSPNPs cleave disulfide bonds and reduce Pt(IV) in high-glutathione (GSH) tumor microenvironment, depleting GSH and releasing active Pt(II) and CA-derivatives. This multi-pronged intervention blocks GSH-dependent cytoprotective hub and synergistically triggers p53-mediated apoptosis, GPX4-related ferroptosis and copper-driven cuproptosis. Compared with CP, the optimal 6bNPs gained 78.7% tumor inhibition in 4T1 xenograft-bearing mice, increased intratumoral Pt-content by 13.5-fold and alleviated systemic toxicity. This study establishes a viable paradigm beyond conventional CP-based chemotherapy and offers a generalizable strategy to enhance the inherent multi-pathway bioactivity of traditional chemotherapeutics.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Pharmacological Characterization of Novel Kappa Opioid Receptor Agonists via Isosteric Replacement Strategy for Inflammatory Pain
item.description:
Abstract
Pain management remains a critical challenge, with mu opioid receptor (MOR) agonists carrying significant risks of respiratory depression and addiction. Kappa opioid receptor (KOR) agonists offer a promising alternative, but centrally mediated adverse effects such as sedation and dysphoria limit their clinical utility. We synthesized 24 nalfurafine analogues via isosteric replacement of its furan side chain with diverse aromatic moieties. All compounds retained high KOR binding affinity and full agonist efficacy, with most displaying G-protein biased signaling. Compound 10, prioritized based on its pharmacological profile, was inactive in thermal nociception assays at doses up to 10 mg/kg, yet produced potent, KOR-mediated antinociception in the acetic acid writhing assay (ED50 = 0.009 mg/kg) and attenuated colonic hypersensitivity in a TNBS-induced colitis model of chronic visceral pain, without significant hypolocomotion. Pharmacokinetic studies identified compound 10 as a P-glycoprotein substrate with limited brain exposure, consistent with a CNS-sparing profile and preferentially peripheral activity.

item.title: Thiophene-Linked Nucleotide Analogues as Selective and Nanomolar Inhibitors of Plasmodial 6-Oxopurine Phosphoribosyltransferases
item.description:
Abstract
6-Oxopurine phosphoribosyltransferases (HGXPRTs) are essential enzymes in the purine salvage pathway of Plasmodium parasites and attractive antimalarial targets. However, the high conservation of their active sites with the human homolog complicates selective inhibitor development. Here, we report thiophene-linked nucleotide analogues as potent and selective inhibitors of plasmodial HG(X)PRTs. Structure-based modeling and conformational analysis guided the incorporation of a rigid thiophene core to control the orientation of phosphate-mimicking groups. C5 sulfonyl substitution markedly enhanced potency, yielding low- to single-digit nanomolar inhibitors of Plasmodium falciparum HGXPRT (PfHGXPRT). Compound 66 emerged as a lead inhibitor (Ki = 7 nM), showing up to ∼3300-fold selectivity over the human enzyme. Compound 63 was the most potent against Plasmodium vivax HGPRT (Ki = 30 nM), highlighting species-dependent linker length effects. Cellular activity remained limited, emphasizing intracellular delivery and/or prodrug activation as key remaining challenges. These compounds establish a promising selective chemotype for further antimalarial development.

item.title: Discovery of Potent and Chemically Diverse PYCR1 Inhibitors with Distinct Binding Sites and Modes of Action
item.description:
Abstract
Pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase 1 (PYCR1) supports tumor growth, stress adaptation, and metastasis but remains an early-stage therapeutic target, with few potent inhibitors and limited knowledge of ligandable sites and modes of action (MoAs). We screened the ∼100,000-compound European Chemical Biology Library and a focused kinase inhibitor collection, identifying 119 validated inhibitors, including several with submicromolar potency and spanning diverse chemotypes. X-ray crystallography showed predominantly non-catalytic-site binding and revealed multiple ligandable regions, including a new pocket enabling covalent targeting of Cys262. At another allosteric site, ligand-induced displacement of Gln10 interfered with NADH binding. Potent PYCR1 inhibitors among kinase inhibitors displayed mostly mixed inhibition kinetics, with one exception acting as an NADH competitor. These findings establish PYCR1 as chemically tractable through diverse MoAs, substantially expand its inhibitor chemical space, and provide starting points for next-generation inhibitors and molecular probes to investigate PYCR1 in cancer-associated metabolic reprogramming.

item.title: Selective Fluorination Affords Hydrophilic Synthetic Glycoconjugates Stable In Vivo
item.description:
Abstract
Therapeutics based on native carbohydrates such as lactose often suffer from short circulation half-lives in vivo due to their rapid clearance from the bloodstream by hepatic C-type lectin receptors, which limits their therapeutic efficacy. A common counter-strategy is to develop structurally distinct glycomimetics by introducing aromatic substituents. However, these modifications often increase hydrophobicity and, in multivalent conjugates, may promote nanoaggregation in the bloodstream, adversely affecting their pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties. In our conceptually distinct approach, strategic fluorine substitution in the native carbohydrate scaffold modulates pharmacokinetics while preserving high water solubility and bioavailability. The prepared highly water-soluble multivalent glycopolymers fluorinated at the 3′- and 4′-positions based on a biocompatible polyoxazoline scaffold exhibited circulation times comparable to the unmodified macromolecular carrier and substantially longer than native lactose-terminated analogues. We establish site-selective carbohydrate fluorination as a broadly applicable platform to improve the pharmacokinetic properties of soluble glycan-based therapeutics, useful for targeting biomedically important lectins, such as β-galactoside-binding galectins.

item.title: A Refined Search of SARS-CoV-2 Main Protease Inhibitors as COVID-19 Antivirals
item.description:
Abstract
MPI8 was among one of the first SARS-CoV-2 main protease (MPro) inhibitors with strong antiviral potency. Building on its peptidomimetic aldehyde scaffold, we retained the P2 3-cyclohexylalanine and P3 O-tert-butylthreonine elements, which support S2 binding, S-subsite engagement, and likely cellular permeability, and varied the S4/S1′ substituents and covalent warheads. SAR and co-crystal structures identified compact N-terminal carbamates or amides bearing cyclopropane, isopropyl, or trifluoromethyl groups as favorable S4 binders. Benzoxazole/benzothiazole-carbonyl groups and acyloxymethyl ketones were explored as S1′-engaging motifs, with one benzoxazole-containing structure confirming tight S1′ packing by crystal structure. Nitrile and 2-amino-2-oxyacetyl warheads provided viable alternatives to the parent aldehyde. Combining optimized S4 groups with alternative warheads or S1′ motifs yielded multiple inhibitors more potent than MPI8. Notably, MPI-131 showed an IC50 of 1.7 nM, strong antiviral potency, and CC50 of 60.2 μM, placing it among the most potent MPro inhibitors reported.

item.title: Discovery of XT1061, a HBV Capsid Assembly Modulator, as a Promising Therapeutic Candidate for Clinical Treatment of HBV Infection
item.description:
Abstract
Hepatitis B virus (HBV) persists as a major unresolved infectious disease. Patients typically require lifelong administration of nucleos(t)ide analogs (NAs) or interferons but seldom achieve functional cure. Recent studies indicate that HBV core assembly modulators (CAMs), when combined with NAs and interferons, can more effectively reduce HBsAg in plasma, thereby facilitating functional cure. In this research, we discovered compound 39 (designated XT1061) through structural optimization of previously reported GLP-26, which exhibited potent anti-HBV activity in vitro (EC50 = 1.0 ± 0.1 nM). In the murine AAV/HBV model, XT1061 induced rapid reduction of HBV DNA and sustained viral DNA clearance throughout treatment. Notably, Combination therapy of XT1061 with pradefovir mesylate (PDV) exhibited significantly enhanced efficacy compared with monotherapy. Further preclinical evaluation and Phase I clinical trials (NCT06280534) confirmed that XT1061 possesses favorable drug-like properties and low safety risks. Collectively, XT1061 represents a promising anti-HBV therapeutic candidate, providing a viable strategy for the clinical management of chronic HBV infection.

item.title: 18 F-Labeled 7-Azaindole-Based Radioligands for Imaging Colony-Stimulating Factor 1 Receptor in Glioblastoma
item.description:
Abstract
A series of 7-azaindole-based compounds were designed and synthesized as novel colony-stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) ligands. Four potent ligands (IC50 < 40 nM) were radiolabeled with fluorine-18 via the 5-fluoroethoxy substituent on the 7-azaindole ring and evaluated comprehensively in rodents and U87MG glioma models. Among them, [18F]PLX6 (IC50 = 12.3 nM) showed modest brain uptake and rapid clearance in rats. Micro-PET/CT imaging resulted in clear visualization of both subcutaneous and intracranial orthotopic U87MG gliomas. Treatment with PLX3397 or PLX5622 significantly reduced tumor uptake, indicating specific binding of [18F]PLX6 to CSF1R. Ex vivo autoradiography at 30 min postinjection (p.i.) confirmed high tumor-to-brain ratio (10.14 ± 1.52) and specific binding of [18F]PLX6 to CSF1R. Metabolic analysis showed that intact [18F]PLX6 was the predominant radioactive species in tumors at 30 min p.i. These results support further evaluation of [18F]PLX6 as a promising PET imaging agent for noninvasive visualization of CSF1R expression in glioblastoma.

item.title: Structure-Based Design of Potent Pan-YTHDF Ligands
item.description:
Abstract
The reader proteins YTHDF1-3 recognize m6A-RNA in the cytosol. Here, we present a structure-based medicinal chemistry campaign that culminated in the pan-YTHDF inhibitor 34 (Kd = 0.14 μM for YTHDF2 by calorimetry), which is selective against YTHDC1 and YTHDC2. The high-resolution crystal structures of the complex of YTHDF2 with six members of the series validate the structure-based design. Using the structural information, we designed compound 31 (IC50 = 0.22 μM for YTHDF2) and a negative control, i.e., its methylated analogue 31b. The cellular thermal shift assay provides evidence of YTHDF2 target engagement in cells for inhibitors 34 and 31, while the negative control 31b is inactive. Compounds 34 and 31 inhibit the proliferation of the AML cell lines MOLM-13 and THP-1. The inhibition of the YTHDF readers by 31 increases the level and stability of the transcript of TNFRSF1B. This renders THP-1 cells more sensitive to TNF-α-induced toxicity.

item.title: From Artificial Intelligence Outputs to Medicinal Chemistry Decisions in Kinase Inhibitor Discovery: Evidence Boundaries, Resistance-Aware Design, and DMTA Learning
item.description:
Abstract
Kinase inhibitor discovery increasingly requires integrated decision-making that extends beyond biochemical potency. Selecting the next analogue, defining the assay package, evaluating structural hypotheses, anticipating resistance, and assessing developability collectively require evidence from distinct experimental layers. In this Perspective, we argue that the practical value of artificial intelligence-assisted drug discovery (AIDD) in kinase inhibitor programs should be assessed not by predictive performance alone but by whether computational outputs improve medicinal chemistry decisions that can be implemented and experimentally tested. We treat AI-supported outputs as testable hypotheses whose value is determined by their effect on analogue selection, assay prioritization, resistance panel design, and information gain across Design−Make−Test−Analyze (DMTA) cycles. Using resistance-focused examples from EGFR, ALK/ROS1/TRK, BCR−ABL1, and BTK, we illustrate how explicit evidence boundaries, validation gates, and falsifying experiments can guide redesign decisions and learning updates.

item.title: An Engineered Heavy-Atom-Free AIE-Active Type-I Sonosensitizer for NIR-II Imaging-Guided Sono-Immunotherapy of Hypoxic Tumors
item.description:
Abstract
The low oxygen dependence of the type-I sonosensitizers renders them promising agents for the treatment of hypoxic solid tumors. However, the rational design of heavy-atom-free type-I sonosensitizers with NIR-II emission remains challenging. Herein, a series of NIR-II heavy-atom-free sonosensitizers were synthesized. Among them, RBT-TPE02 exhibited pronounced aggregation-induced emission (AIE) characteristics, good NIR-II fluorescence, and efficient type-I reactive oxygen species generation under ultrasound irradiation. After nanoformulation, RBT-TPE02 NPs demonstrated notable type-I sonodynamic therapy (SDT) activity, which enabled efficient inhibition of tumor cells under hypoxic conditions and induced pyroptosis-associated immunogenic cell death upon ultrasound irradiation. In vivo experiments further confirmed that RBT-TPE02 NPs mediated efficient NIR-II imaging-guided SDT, resulting in effective tumor suppression and the activation of anti-tumor immune responses. This work presents a heavy-atom-free AIEgen engineering strategy that integrates NIR-II fluorescence, oxygen-independent type-I sonodynamic action, and pyroptosis-mediated immune activation in a single molecular platform for imaging-guided tumor therapy under hypoxia.

item.title: Discovery of 2-(Phenylamino)-6 H -pyrimido[5,4- b ][1,4]oxazin-7(8 H )-one Derivatives as Selective ACK1 Inhibitors with Immunomodulatory Effects Enhancing Anti-PD-1 Therapy for Triple-Negative Breast Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive subtype with limited therapeutic options due to the lack of actionable targets. ACK1 contributes to tumor progression and immune evasion, representing a promising immunomodulatory target whose inhibition can potentiate anti-PD-1 therapy in TNBC. Herein, we report the discovery and structure−activity relationship (SAR) of 2-(phenylamino)-6H-pyrimido[5,4-b][1,4]oxazin-7(8H)-one derivatives as a new class of ACK1 inhibitors. The optimized compound 20l potently inhibits ACK1 (IC50 = 1 nM) and its autophosphorylation in TNBC cells. In vitro, 20l suppresses TNBC cell proliferation, migration, and invasion while inducing cell cycle arrest and apoptosis. In vivo, 20l not only directly inhibits TNBC cell growth but also remodels the immune microenvironment and activates systemic immunity. Combined treatment with 20l and an anti-PD-1 antibody produced a TGI of 95.7% without evident toxicity. Thus, 20l represents a promising ACK1-targeted therapeutic lead that warrants further investigation for the treatment of aggressive TNBC.

item.title: Discovery and Structural Optimization of Elephantopus scaber -Derived Sesquiterpene Lactones as Covalent PRDX6 Inhibitors for Colorectal Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a highly aggressive malignancy, highlighting the need for therapeutic agents with distinct mechanisms of action. Natural products provide structurally diverse and biologically privileged scaffolds for anticancer drug discovery. Building on an anti-CRC germacrane-type sesquiterpene lactone scaffold (SC) isolated from Elephantopus scaber Linn., we identified PRDX6 as a covalent target using a biotinylated probe and covalent mass spectrometry, which revealed engagement of the catalytic residue Cys47. Structure-guided C6 functionalization with a 1,2,3-triazole motif afforded compound 1c, which showed enhanced PRDX6 binding, inhibited PRDX6 enzymatic activity, and promoted intracellular ROS accumulation, leading to potent anti-CRC effects. To improve in vivo developability, a morpholine hydrochloride prodrug, 6c, was designed and synthesized. Compound 6c displayed favorable pharmacokinetic properties, efficient systemic release of 1c, and significant antitumor efficacy in CRC xenograft models. This study establishes SC-derived sesquiterpene lactones as promising natural product-based covalent PRDX6 inhibitors for CRC drug discovery.

item.title: Discovery of Nivegacetor, an Advanced γ-Secretase Modulator, for the Treatment of Alzheimer’s Disease
item.description:
Abstract
Recent clinical data regarding amyloid-beta (Aβ) antibodies support the validity of reducing Aβ-amyloidosis or aggregated Aβ as a disease-modifying therapy for Alzheimer’s disease (AD). γ-Secretase (GS) remains an important target for the treatment of AD, and its pharmacological modulation, instead of inhibition, can deliver a safe treatment. Following extensive efforts to optimize the pharmacological and physicochemical properties (e.g., potency, selectivity, and solubility) of our previous clinical candidate, RO7185876, and to mitigate safety findings observed during advanced toxicology studies, we successfully identified RG6289 (nivegacetor). Herein, we report the comprehensive optimization process and the exploration of multiple chemical subseries that led to the discovery of the nivegacetor. Currently in Phase II clinical trials, nivegacetor is characterized by an improved safety profile and holds the potential to halt or delay amyloid accumulation and become an orally administered disease-modifying therapy for the treatment of AD.

item.title: Thiazolidinones as Potential Inhibitors to Target RPB12 for Treatment of Colorectal Cancer Growth
item.description:
Abstract
Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains a major cause of cancer-related mortality worldwide, and selective molecular targets and corresponding inhibitors remain insufficiently developed. Starting from a phenotypic screening hit, we performed systematic structural optimization guided by metabolism-guided modification, leading to the discovery of B9. B9 selectively inhibited HCT116 CRC cells and showed much weaker inhibition of normal colonic epithelial NCM460 cells (IC50 = 0.052 vs 1.114 μM). B9 also suppressed CRC clonogenic growth, 3D spheroid formation, and migration- and invasion-associated phenotypes in vitro. B9 achieved significant tumor growth inhibition (TGI = 80.1%) in vivo without obvious toxicity. RPB12 was identified as a candidate cellular target of B9 by activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) and validated by shRNA knockdown, CETSA, DARTS, SPR, and molecular docking. These findings support RPB12 as a novel promising target for the treatment of CRC and B9 as the first RPB12-targeting inhibitor for further development in CRC therapy.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Evaluation of Cyclopropyl-Based PD-1/PD-L1 Interaction Inhibitors Bearing a Dipeptide Tail with Improved Drug-likeness
item.description:
Abstract
Small-molecule blockade of PD-1/PD-L1 offers a promising strategy for cancer immunotherapy, although combining potent inhibition with favorable drug-like properties remains challenging. Herein, hydrophilic substituents were introduced into the solvent-exposed region of a biphenyl scaffold using a stereochemically defined cyclopropyl linker. The cyclopropyl linker enabled systematic variation of amino alcohol, amino acid, dipeptide, and peptidomimetic polar groups. Systematic structure−activity relationship studies identified the dipeptide-derived (1S,2S)-F33 as a potent inhibitor of PD-1/PD-L1 binding (IC50 = 1.6 nM) with high affinity for PD-L1 (KD = 0.16 μM). The compound exhibited improved aqueous solubility and liver microsomal stability, with an oral bioavailability of 28.29% in mice. Oral administration of (1S,2S)-F33 dose-dependently suppressed tumor growth in a B16−F10 melanoma mouse model, achieving 73.69% tumor growth inhibition, accompanied by enhanced antitumor immune responses and favorable tolerability. Collectively, these findings establish (1S,2S)-F33 as a promising lead for the further development of drug-like small-molecule PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors.

item.title: DCLK1-Targeting PROTAC as a Therapeutic Strategy for Acute Lung Injury: Inhibition of Pro-inflammatory Macrophage Polarization
item.description:
Abstract
Doublecortin-like kinase 1 (DCLK1) has emerged as a promising therapeutic target in acute inflammatory diseases. Despite DCLK1’s emerging role in acute lung injury (ALI), conventional occupancy-driven inhibitors face limitations in efficacy and potential toxicity. Herein, we designed and synthesized the first series of DCLK1-targeting proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs). Among them, compound D11 potently degraded DCLK1 via the ubiquitin-proteasome system, with DC50 values of 36.93 nM and 75.67 nM in RAW264.7 and THP-1 cells, respectively. D11 effectively suppressed lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced macrophage M1 polarization in vitro and reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production. In LPS-induced acute lung injury (ALI) model, D11 administration significantly attenuated lung pathology, decreased inflammatory cell infiltration, lowered cytokine levels, and inhibited pulmonary M1 macrophage polarization with no detectable toxicity. These findings demonstrate that targeted degradation of DCLK1 via PROTAC represents a viable and effective strategy for treating ALI, highlighting D11 as a promising lead compound for further development.

item.title: Discovery of Zoldonrasib (RMC-9805), a Potent and Orally Bioavailable RAS(ON) G12D-Selective, Covalent, Tri-Complex Inhibitor for the Treatment of Patients with RAS G12D-Addicted Cancers
item.description:
Abstract
RAS mutations are among the most frequent oncogenic drivers in human cancer, and KRAS G12D is one of the most prevalent RAS alterations occurring in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), colorectal cancer (CRC), and non-small cell lung cancer. Here, we describe the structure-based SAR journey that led to the discovery of zoldonrasib (RMC-9805), an orally bioavailable RAS(ON) G12D-selective, covalent, tri-complex inhibitor. Discovery of an aziridine-2-carboxamide-based warhead and a rigid spirocyclic linker enabled selective covalent engagement of KRAS G12D in its active, GTP-bound state. Zoldonrasib exhibited potent inhibition of KRAS G12D signaling and proliferation in KRAS G12D-dependent cancer cells, favorable ADME and cross-species pharmacokinetic properties, and selectivity over RAS-independent cellular models. In vivo, zoldonrasib produced deep and durable suppression of tumor RAS pathway signaling and induced dose-dependent tumor regressions in KRAS G12D-driven xenograft models. Currently, zoldonrasib is in clinical evaluation for KRAS G12D mutant solid tumors.

item.title: Discovery of RMC-0708, an Oral, Bis-Macrocyclic, RAS(ON) Q61H-Selective, Noncovalent, Tri-Complex Inhibitor
item.description:
Abstract
Oncogenic RAS mutations are among the most common drivers of human cancers, with the KRAS Q61H mutation accounting for approximately 7500 new patients each year in the US alone. To target the active, GTP-bound state of the KRAS(ON) Q61H mutant protein directly, we have employed an innovative tri-complex inhibitor (TCI) modality. Herein, we report structure-guided medicinal chemistry efforts that led to the discovery of RMC-0708, an orally bioavailable, bis-macrocyclic, RAS(ON) Q61H-selective, noncovalent, tri-complex inhibitor. Oral administration of a single dose of RMC-0708 resulted in dose-dependent, deep, and durable suppression of tumor RAS pathway activity for up to 72 h in preclinical xenograft models of KRAS Q61H-driven cancers in vivo. RMC-0708 drove deep tumor regressions in several xenograft models of human KRAS Q61H mutant tumors. The discovery of RMC-0708 further underscores the potential of the TCI platform to identify potent and selective noncovalent inhibitors of mutant RAS(ON) with demonstrated selectivity over wild-type RAS.

item.title: Discovery of Orally Effective Corydamine Derivatives Targeting Glutathione Metabolism to Sensitize Hepatocellular Carcinoma to Sorafenib
item.description:
Abstract
Sorafenib offers limited benefit in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). In this study, we designed and synthesized a series of novel corydamine derivatives and identified 8g as a lead compound with anti-HCC activity comparable to sorafenib. Mechanistic studies suggest that 8g targets glutathione reductase (GR), disrupting glutathione metabolism and NADPH homeostasis and weakening tumor redox defenses. Notably, the combination of 8g and sorafenib markedly enhanced ROS generation, inhibited HCC cell migration and invasion, and induced G2/M arrest and apoptosis, demonstrating strong synergistic anticancer activity. In addition, 8g showed favorable druggability, including good metabolic stability in human liver microsomes (T1/2 > 5 h), low hERG inhibition (IC50 > 50 μM), and high oral bioavailability (84.9%). In a Huh7 xenograft model, the combination achieved 61.0% tumor growth inhibition, significantly outperforming sorafenib alone (29.7%). These findings propose a redox-targeting strategy to sensitize HCC to sorafenib and highlight 8g as a promising anti-HCC lead.

item.title: Enhanced Pulmonary Fibrosis Treatment by Self-Assembling Peptide Nanofibers via Improved Pulmonary Delivery and Retention
item.description:
Abstract
Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is a life-threatening interstitial lung disease, which progressively impairs pulmonary function, with limited therapeutic options available. In this study, we designed CQ7, a self-assembling peptide that integrates a therapeutic peptide with a self-assembly motif. CQ7 monomers spontaneously form supramolecular nanofibers under physiological conditions, both extracellularly and intracellularly. This nanofiber structure promotes efficient lung retention and targeted pulmonary delivery, leading to enhanced anti-fibrotic efficacy. We evaluated the anti-fibrotic and anti-inflammatory effects of CQ7 in a murine PF model via both intraperitoneal and inhalation administrations. Transcriptomic sequencing and experimental validation further revealed that CQ7 may act through the regulation of mitochondrial function, reducing cellular oxidative stress and thereby regulating the apoptosis process. Collectively, this work demonstrates a novel peptide-based strategy with significant potential for improving PF outcomes and clinical translation.

item.title: Call for Papers: Advances and Challenges in DMPK in Drug Discovery
Discovery of 7-Aminofuro[2,3- c ]pyridine-Based Irreversible Inhibitors of TGFβ-Activated Kinase 1 (TAK1) with In Vivo Antitumor Activity
item.description:
Abstract
TGFβ-activated kinase 1 (TAK1) plays essential roles in proinflammatory and prosurvival signaling pathways, and has been implicated in various human diseases, including cancer and inflammation. Although several TAK1 inhibitors have been reported, an effective tool compound with a combination of favorable potency, selectivity, and in vivo efficacy is still lacking. Herein, we present a 7-aminofuro[2,3-c]pyridine-based α,β-unsaturated aldehyde (compound 26) as a potent TAK1 irreversible covalent inhibitor. This compound exhibited excellent inhibitory activity for TAK1-dependent signaling in cells and demonstrated a sustained TAK1 inhibition effect in vivo. Furthermore, it significantly prevented tumor growth in a lymphoma (DoHH2) xenograft mouse model. Although a contribution from the inhibition of other kinases to the observed effects cannot be ruled out, compound 26 provides a promising starting point for further optimization of TAK1 selectivity and pharmacokinetic properties toward the development of TAK1-targeted agents.

item.title: Structure-Guided Discovery of Non-Peptide Macrocyclic KEAP1−NRF2 Inhibitors Targeting Cuproptosis in Depression
item.description:
Abstract
Macrocyclic molecules are promising for targeting intractable protein−protein interactions (PPIs). The small-molecule KEAP1−NRF2 PPI inhibitors have shown potential for treating major depressive disorder (MDD). Herein, we report a crystallographic structure-guided strategy for the design of non-peptide macrocyclic KEAP1−NRF2 PPI inhibitors. The best macrocyclic compound T7 exhibits rapid binding and slow dissociation with the KEAP1 protein, significant in vitro anti-oxidative stress and anti-inflammatory activities, and capacity for brain penetration. In a chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) mouse model, T7 treatment improves the depressive behavior and serum neurotransmitter levels by activating the NRF2 pathway. Furthermore, we found that the activation suppresses CUMS-induced cuproptotic pathologies including mitochondrial morphological disruption/reduced density, synaptic vesicle depletion, and dysregulated expression of cuproptosis mediators in hippocampal and cortical regions. Collectively, our study presents a structure-based strategy to develop macrocyclic KEAP1−NRF2 PPI inhibitors, which hold promise for treating MDD by engaging NRF2-mediated cuproptosis suppression in stress-related neuropathology.

item.title: Fluorine-Functionalized Isophorone Near-Infrared Cu 2+ Fluorescent Probe for Lung-Targeted Imaging of Diabetic Lung Injury and Lung Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Traditional small-molecule fluorescent probes suffer from nonspecific accumulation in metabolic organs, limiting their application in lung disease monitoring. Herein, we developed a fluorine-substituted dicyanoisophorone-based probe (PFCu) with picolinate as the Cu2+-recognition moiety. PFCu preferentially illuminated A549 cancer cells and exhibited remarkable lung-targeting accumulation, enabling specific Cu2+ recognition in the lung. The probe allows real-time monitoring of Cu2+ level in living cells and possesses ER-targeting ability, facilitating analysis of Cu2+ fluctuations in high glucose-induced diabetic models and revealing the relationship among hyperglycemia, ER stress, and copper homeostasis. Notably, PFCu effectively distinguished lung tumor-bearing mice from healthy controls and showed significantly higher fluorescence in tumor tissues than in adjacent normal tissues from clinical samples. This study provides a novel molecular tool for lung disease research, supports Cu2+ as a potential biomarker for early diagnosis of lung cancer, and offers new strategies for diagnosing Cu2+-related diseases.

item.title: Discovery of INCB161734: A Selective Inhibitor of the KRAS G12D Mutant
item.description:
Abstract
The discovery of the clinical KRAS G12D inhibitor INCB161734 is described. Starting from a previously disclosed orally bioavailable tool compound 1, a concerted effort to improve the predicted human dose via modulation of potency and pharmacokinetics was undertaken. Careful consideration of the metabolic profile was key to designing low clearance compounds. In addition, the molecular size and fraction sp3 character were carefully controlled to improve permeability and crystalline solubility. From this effort, INCB161734 was identified as a balanced compound with excellent oral exposure, potent antiproliferative activity in xenograft tumor models, and excellent selectivity against wild-type K/H/NRAS. INCB161734 is currently undergoing clinical trials in patients with KRAS G12D mutations.

item.title: Democratizing Drug Discovery: A Scalable Open-Source Pipeline for Massive Specific Protein Target QSAR Modeling Using ChEMBL
item.description:
Abstract
The proprietary nature of AI/ML tools in drug discovery limits access to advanced virtual screening methodologies. To address this, we present an open-source, automated pipeline for large-scale Quantitative Structure−Activity Relationship (QSAR) modeling utilizing ChEMBL. Our batch processing system constructed 2263 predictive models across multiple protein targets, applying both regression and classification strategies with strict quality control thresholds. The pipeline integrates ErG and RDKit descriptor families, employs Random Forest and XGBoost algorithms with Optuna-based hyperparameter optimization, and handles class imbalances using SMOTE. Models are saved only when achieving R2 ≥ 0.7 for regression or MCC ≥ 0.55 for classification. Data is stratified by assay and measurement types to maintain biological relevance. Additionally, we feature an interactive EDA visualization tool with ErG heatmaps and external validation via the DELTA database. This work democratizes industrial-grade QSAR infrastructure, empowering the research community to reproduce and extend computational workflows.

item.title: Triskellines A (3,6,8-Trisubstituted [1,2,4]triazolo[4,3- b ]pyridazines) as Potent Antagonists of Human Adenosine Receptor A3
item.description:
Abstract
Adenosine receptor A3 (A3AR) is coupled to Gi proteins, leading to adenylate cyclase inhibition, and to Go proteins, leading to phospholipase C activation and Ca++ release. We here describe the synthesis and biological characterization of a family of 3,6,8-trisubstituted [1,2,4]-triazolo-[4,3-b]-pyridazines (Triskellines A), initially inspired from the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitory purine (R)-Roscovitine. Triskellines A act as selective A3AR antagonists. Among 234 synthesized compounds, some display extremely potent binding activity (2-digit picomolar IC50 values in a human A3AR agonist radioligand binding assay) and very high selectivity toward A3AR compared to adenosine receptors A1AR, A2AAR, and A2BAR (4-Log difference in IC50 values). Triskellines A do not inhibit protein kinases. A structure−activity relationship study points toward optimal potency structural features. Molecular docking with A3AR reveals interaction of Triskellines in the adenosine binding pocket at the agonist drug Piclidenoson (IB-MECA) binding site. Triskelline A-143 displays favorable pharmacological and safety properties.

item.title: Preclinical Characterization of [ 68 Ga]Ga/[ 177 Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB: A Dual-Targeted Agent against PSMA and NTSR1 for Prostate Cancer Theranostics
item.description:
Abstract
Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) is a key biomarker for prostate cancer (PCa), while neurotensin receptor 1 (NTSR1) is positive in PSMA-negative PCa lesions. For comprehensive diagnosis and therapy of PCa, we synthesized dual-targeted PSNT-AB (combining PSMA-targeted EuK, NTSR1-targeted NT-20.3, albumin-binding 4-p-tolylbutyric acid and DOTA moieties) and prepared [68Ga]Ga/[177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB. [68Ga]Ga-PSNT-AB possessed high affinity for PSMA-positive LNCaP and moderate affinity for NTSR1-positive PC-3 cells. Probes accumulated time-dependently in relevant cells, and [177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB exerted potent cytotoxicity. Pharmacokinetics revealed prolonged blood half-lives for both probes. PET imaging revealed persistent [68Ga]Ga-PSNT-AB uptake in LNCaP, 22Rv1 and PC-3 tumors (10.29 ± 0.25% ID/g, 6.61 ± 0.30% ID/g, 3.74 ± 0.12% ID/g at 3 h post-injection). SPECT/CT showed sustained [177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB retention in LNCaP tumors for at least 24 h. These results demonstrated that [68Ga]Ga/[177Lu]Lu-PSNT-AB are promising dual-targeted probes for PCa diagnosis and therapy, offering a potential strategy for comprehensive and effective precision management of PCa.

item.title: Rationally Designed TLR2-QS-21 Liposomal Adjuvant Enhances Immunogenicity while Reducing Reactogenicity in Subunit Vaccines
item.description:
Abstract
Potent vaccine adjuvants often link strong adaptive immunity with excessive inflammation. Here, we developed BQS01, a liposomal adjuvant that replaces the TLR4 agonist monophosphoryl lipid A (MPL) with a synthetic TLR2 agonist (BXY-14) while retaining QS-21. BQS01 induced a TLR2-associated transcriptional profile, enhanced dendritic cell activation and T-cell priming, and was associated with increased IL-10 production. In ovalbumin and varicella-zoster virus mouse models, BQS01 generated antibody responses comparable to an AS01b-like MPL/QS-21 comparator and durable polyfunctional cellular immunity, while reducing systemic weight loss, local inflammation, and TNF-α accumulation. These findings suggest that innate signaling architecture, rather than inflammatory magnitude alone, contributes to adjuvant performance and may guide the design of next-generation vaccines with an improved immunogenicity−reactogenicity balance.

item.title: A Molecular Design Strategy for Light-on Photoswitchable β-Adrenoceptors Agonists with Tailored Photochemical Properties and Distinct Efficacy Profiles
item.description:
Abstract
Despite significant advances in β-adrenoceptor photopharmacology, no photoswitchable agonists have been reported with a fully inactive trans isomer that can be reversibly activated by light. Herein, we present a novel chemical design for the development of light-regulated β1-AR agonists that selectively activate β1-AR upon illumination. Using an azologization strategy based on BI-167107 and Cimaterol, we synthesized and characterized a series of β1-AR-targeting photoswitchable molecules. This approach yielded light-on agonists responsive to both UV and visible light, displaying distinct thermal relaxation kinetics and efficacy profiles. Overall, this study outlines a design strategy that enables the development of drugs targeting these widely studied therapeutic receptors with optimized photochemical and pharmacological properties through structural modification of the core scaffold. These new classes of compounds may serve as future therapeutic agents that can be activated at specific locations and for precisely controlled durations, thereby minimizing off-target effects and systemic side effects.

item.title: Discovery of a Novel Pyrido[2,1- h ]pteridin-6-one Derivative as a Potent and Orally Bioavailable HPK1 Inhibitor
item.description:
Abstract
Hematopoietic progenitor kinase 1 (HPK1), a key negative regulator of T-cell activation, represents a highly promising yet challenging target for cancer immunotherapy. To date, no HPK1 inhibitor has received marketing approval, underscoring the need for innovative scaffolds. Here, we report the structure-based drug discovery of a potent HPK1 inhibitor featuring a unique pyrido[2,1-h]pteridin-6-one core. Through a series of chemical modifications, including scaffold hopping and ring-system optimization, starting from a known diaminopyrimidine carboxamide structure, we successfully constructed this key tricyclic core. The lead compound 29 exhibited remarkable potency against HPK1, along with outstanding selectivity. It effectively suppressed HPK1-mediated SLP-76 phosphorylation, thereby enhancing T-cell activation in both Jurkat cells and human PBMCs. Moreover, 29 displayed excellent oral bioavailability and markedly enhanced antitumor efficacy in combination with anti-PD-1 in a CT26.WT syngeneic mouse model. Collectively, these findings identify a novel, potent, and selective HPK1 inhibitor, offering a promising candidate for advancing cancer immunotherapy.

item.title: Synthesis and Preclinical Evaluation of a Novel Technetium-99m-Labeled Tracer for Tumor Hypoxia Imaging with Low Uptake in the Intestines and Liver
item.description:
Abstract
Hypoxia imaging can provide crucial information for clinical tumor treatment decisions. To decrease the excessive abdominal uptake in nontarget organs of radiotracers and obtain high imaging contrast, two 2-nitroimidazole derivatives (2NMDPro and 2NMLPro) modified with different proline linkers were designed and synthesized. Six complexes with good in vitro stability were acquired by radiolabeling with technetium-99m and various coligands. Among them, [99mTc]Tc-2NMDPro-M1 exhibited good hypoxic selectivity in vitro S180 cell uptake, good hydrophilicity (log D7.4 = −2.87 ± 0.03), high tumor uptake (1.01 ± 0.13 ID %/g, 1 h postinjection, p.i.), and low uptake in intestines and liver (0.33 ± 0.06 ID %/g and 0.65 ± 0.15 ID %/g, respectively, 1 h p.i.) in S180 tumor-bearing mice biodistribution and SPECT/CT imaging study. Ex vivo radioautography and immunohistochemical (IHC) staining of the HIF-1α study also confirmed the selective accumulation of [99mTc]Tc-2NMDPro-M1 in the hypoxia area. Consequently, [99mTc]Tc-2NMDPro-M1 is a highly potential tracer for tumor hypoxia imaging in clinical nuclear medicine.

item.title: New Phenazine 5,10-Dioxide Carbamates Inspired by Iodinin and Myxin Exhibit Improved Potency in Human Leukemia Cells with High Cytotoxic Selectivity, Activity against Mycobacterium Tuberculosis and Low Toxicity to Zebrafish Larvae
item.description:
Abstract
Myxin and iodinin are phenazines known for antileukemic- and antimicrobial effects. Herein, we synthesized carbamate derivatives from an iodinin regioisomer and assessed their cytotoxicity in vitro toward leukemic and tubercular cells, as well as non-cancerous NRK and H9c2 cells, and evaluated their in vivo toxicity in zebrafish larvae. Myxin’ s antileukemic potency of 1.4 μM IC50 (MOLM-13 cells) was outperformed by several carbamate derivatives, including a methylsulfonyl-imidazolidinone analog (21) showing IC50 of 0.26 μM. The analogs showed large variation in cytotoxic selectivity toward MOLM-13 over normal cells, and in zebrafish larvae toxicity. An imidazolidinone derivative (22) was identified to be particularly favorable, combining high antileukemic- and antitubercular potency with low cytotoxicity to non-cancerous cells and undetected zebrafish toxicity at 200 μM. Furthermore, this derivative was less prone to liver metabolism than myxin. The findings establish carbamate functionalization as a promising strategy for developing new antileukemic and antitubercular phenazines.

item.title: Mitochondria-Targeted Iridium(III) Complexes Entrapped in Liposomes Induce Cell Death through Ferroptosis
item.description:
Abstract
The anticancer efficacy of iridium(III) complexes has been extensively studied. A new ligand TFMPIP (2-(4-(trifluoromethoxy)phenyl)-1H-imidazo[4,5-f][1,10]phenanthroline) and its four iridium(III) complexes [Ir(C−N)2(TFMPIP)]PF6 (C−N = ppy: 13a, bzq: 13b, piq: 13c, and dfppy: 13d) were synthesized and characterized. The complexes show moderate or low cytotoxicity against LA795, HCT116, and Huh7 cells, while their liposome formulations 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo significantly enhanced the antiproliferative activity against LA795 cells. Mechanistic investigations revealed that 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo accumulated in mitochondria and induced pronounced mitochondrial dysfunction. Subsequent experiments confirmed that 13a@lipo, 13b@lipo, 13c@lipo, and 13d@lipo triggered apoptosis, suppressed the PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling pathway, and induced ferroptosis. In vivo antitumor activity showed that 13c@lipo significantly inhibited tumor growth in the LA795 tumor-bearing model with a high inhibitory rate of 82.72%. Collectively, these findings identify 13c@lipo as a promising liposomal Ir(III)-based candidate for lung adenocarcinoma therapy.

item.title: Synthesis, Structure−Property Relationships, and Photodynamic Activity of Heavy-Atom-Free BODIPY Photosensitizers Based on Spin−Orbit Charge Transfer
item.description:
Abstract
The geometrically orthogonal donor−acceptor (D−A) architecture, which favors spin−orbit charge-transfer intersystem crossing (SOCT-ISC), has emerged as a promising strategy for developing heavy-atom-free photosensitizers. However, systematic structure−property relationship (SPR) studies for such systems remain limited. In this work, we designed and synthesized 18 orthogonal D−A BODIPY derivatives modified with diverse electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups. SPR investigation established that the meso-anthryl moiety and quaternary ammonium groups at the 3,5- and 2,6-positions significantly enhanced D−A interaction, reduced ΔEST, strengthened spin−orbit coupling (SOC), and thereby promoted SOCT-ISC, leading to markedly increased ROS generation (∼20-fold vs Chlorin e6). Importantly, the optimized compound An-DQA-OM, formulated as nanoparticles (ADO NPs), exhibited potent oxygen-independent photocytotoxicity (IC50 ≈ 0.39 μM in normoxia and 0.79 μM in hypoxia) and strong in vivo antitumor efficacy. This work presented a SPR paradigm for the rational design of efficient, heavy-atom-free BODIPY photosensitizers via the SOCT-ISC mechanism.

item.title: Chemical Determinants of Spinal Analgesia in NTS2-Selective Macrocycles
item.description:
Abstract
Neurotensin (NT)-based ligands represent promising non-opioid analgesics. Here, we designed and synthesized a focused library of macrocyclic NT analogs combining substitutions previously shown to enhance NTS2 affinity, selectivity, and/or antinociceptive activity. Several macrocycles retained low-nanomolar NTS2 affinity and remarkable subtype selectivity, including analog M19, which exhibited >53,000-fold selectivity over NTS1, the highest reported to date. Although combining favorable substitutions did not produce additive improvements, M19 and M25 displayed potent spinal antinociceptive activity in rat tail-flick and formalin tests. Most importantly, removal of the N-terminal amine abolished antinociceptive activity while preserving high NTS2 affinity, identifying this pharmacophore as a critical determinant of NTS2-mediated analgesia. Molecular dynamics simulations comparing M25 with its desamino analog M29 revealed distinct extracellular interaction networks and conformational dynamics, including the loss of prominent ECL2-N-terminal and ECL3 interactions in M29. These findings provide a structural framework for the rational development of selective, non-opioid analgesics targeting NTS2.

item.title: Salicylamides as RNA-Dependent RNA Polymerase Inhibitors with Antiviral Activity against West Nile and Zika Viruses
item.description:
Abstract
Mosquito-transmitted orthoflaviviruses constitute an escalating global threat to public health, for which no approved antiviral therapies exist. Here, we identify the salicylanilide derivative S1 as a West Nile virus (WNV) RNA-dependent RNA-polymerase (RdRp) inhibitor. Chemical optimization of S1 yielded compound S7, which inhibited WNV RdRp activity and displayed antiviral efficacy in Vero cells (EC50 of 3.0 μM; CC50 > 100 μM). S7 and related analogues inhibited Zika virus (ZIKV) RdRp, and this enzymatic inhibition translated into antiviral activity in cell-based assays. Compared with niclosamide, as reference salicylanilide, compound S7 exerted lower impact on mitochondria, reduced cytotoxicity and no induction of apoptosis. Molecular modelling support binding within the polymerase N-pocket, with key contributing residues being highly conserved in both WNV and ZIKV polymerases. Site-directed mutagenesis further supported the importance of N-pocket residues for S7 binding. Therefore, the S7-scaffold constitutes a promising antiviral chemotype against orthoflaviviruses.

item.title: Identification and Development of Pyrano[2,3- c ]Pyrazole-Based Scaffold for Selective Human Carbonic Anhydrase IX Inhibition
item.description:
Abstract
The high structural similarity among the human Carbonic Anhydrase (hCA) isoforms represents a major challenge for developing selective inhibitors for targeted anticancer therapies. Herein, we report the design, synthesis, biological assessment, and mechanistic investigation of a series of pyrano[2,3-c]pyrazole derivatives as hCA inhibitors. The most active compounds displayed remarkable inhibitory potency and selectivity toward hCAIX, with compound 12 emerging as the most promising derivative, whose binding mode was further rationalized through computational studies. Notably, compound 12, in combination with the GPX4 inhibitor RSL3, demonstrated a synergistic effect in pancreatic cancer cell lines. Moreover, this lead exhibited a potential role in regulating cell migration and ultrastructural studies suggested changes in the expression pattern of markers related to autophagy, metabolism, and EMT associated processes. Overall, these findings identify pyrano[2,3-c]pyrazoles as promising hCAIX-selective chemotypes for targeting hypoxia-associated tumor adaptation and combination anticancer strategies aimed at limiting tumor progression and metastatic dissemination.

item.title: Discovery of Potent and Non-cytotoxic HDAC3-Selective Degraders Featuring a Propyl Hydrazide Zinc-Binding Group
item.description:
Abstract
Histone deacetylase 3 (HDAC3) is an important therapeutic target in cancer, yet selective HDAC3 degraders remain limited. In this study, we report the development of novel class I HDAC degraders derived from the HDAC3-preferential inhibitor FL-007. Two linker exit vectors were investigated, leading to the identification of a series of potent compounds (2a−d) exhibiting low micromolar inhibition of HDAC2 and submicromolar inhibition of HDAC1 and HDAC3, together with selective HDAC3 degradation. Degradation activity was confirmed in MM.1S, HCT116, A2780-HDAC3-HiBiT, and Cal27CisR cells using immunoblotting and HiBiT/LgBiT assays, achieving Dmax values of up to 92%. Notably, these compounds showed no cytotoxicity up to 100 μM in both cancerous and non-cancerous cell lines. Selective HDAC3 degradation resulted in moderate chemosensitization of cisplatin-resistant Cal27CisR cells, in contrast to the stronger effects observed with cytotoxic HDAC inhibitors. For compound 2b, the chemosensitizing effect was associated with increased histone H3 acetylation and increased p21 expression.

item.title: Discovery of a Highly Potent and Selective Oncolytic Peptide NF27 through Structure−Activity Relationship Studies
item.description:
Abstract
Oncolytic peptides specifically induce cancer cell death by rupturing the cell membrane, but their structure−activity relationship (SAR) remains poorly understood and no peptides have been clinically approved. Here, we designed and evaluated CKS1-derived peptides to identify key SAR features, including the role of a proline-induced hinge and the spatial distribution of hydrophilic and hydrophobic amino acids. Among them, NF27 showed potent and broad anticancer activity with minimal toxicity toward healthy cells and low hemolysis. Mechanistic studies revealed that cell size and cell−cell junctions correlate with sensitivity to oncolytic peptides. NF27-induced cell death was immunogenic and promoted infiltration of immune cells in murine tumors. In murine tumor models, NF27 effectively suppressed tumor growth and achieved complete eradication in some cases, with no observable systemic toxicity. These findings establish fundamental SAR principles for oncolytic peptides and identify NF27 as a promising therapeutic candidate.

item.title: Lysosome-Targeted Iridium(III)-BODIPY Conjugates with GSH-Activatable Reactive Oxygen Species Generation for Enhanced Photodynamic Immunotherapy of Melanoma
item.description:
Abstract
Melanoma represents a major clinical challenge due to its aggressive nature, high metastatic potential, and resistance to conventional therapies. Herein, we developed two near-infrared iridium(III)-BODIPY conjugates (BODIPY-1-Ir and BODIPY-2-Ir) for glutathione (GSH)-activated photodynamic immunotherapy. These conjugates function as lysosome-targeting photosensitizers that deplete intracellular GSH to disrupt redox balance and enhance reactive oxygen species generation with light irradiation. The phototoxicity further induces cascading dendritic cell maturation and tumor-associated macrophage reprogramming, promoting immunogenic cell death. Both in vitro and in vivo studies demonstrated their excellent biocompatibility, strong photodynamic anticancer efficiency, and significant tumor growth inhibition, highlighting their potential as promising candidates for melanoma treatment.

item.title: Evaluation and an Exploratory Human Study of 99m Tc-Labeled PSMA-Targeting Agents with Reduced Renal Uptake via Proline Incorporation
item.description:
Abstract
Excessive renal uptake of prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA)-targeted radiopharmaceuticals remains a major challenge in prostate cancer (PCa) detection and therapy. We developed 99mTc-labeled PSMA radioligands incorporating d- or l-proline as a conformationally constrained linker combined with optimized co-ligands to reduce kidney accumulation. The resulting hydrophilic complexes achieved high radiochemical yields and strong in vitro stability. The optimal radiotracer, [99mTc]Tc-L-M1, exhibited high LNCaP (PSMA++) cell affinity (Kd = 19.09 nM) and the lowest kidney uptake (6.50 ± 0.32% ID/g, Kunming mice, 2 h p.i.). It accumulated effectively in both LNCaP (PSMA++) and 22Rv1 (PSMA+) tumors with excellent target-to-nontarget ratios and strong PSMA specificity. SPECT/CT imaging confirmed low renal accumulation, consistent with biodistribution data. Preliminary clinical trials demonstrated clear delineation of small PCa lesions, highlighting [99mTc]Tc-L-M1 as a promising PSMA-specific radiotracer with reduced kidney uptake for clinical application.

item.title: Rational Design of Potent and Highly Selective FGFR1 Irreversible Inhibitors Guided by Molecular Dynamics Simulations
item.description:
Abstract
Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations revealed distinct P-loop conformational differences in the ATP-binding domain between FGFR1 and other FGFR subtypes. A conformation-restricted linker optimization strategy was applied to identify a potent and selective irreversible FGFR1 inhibitor (compound 24). MD models demonstrated that the covalent warhead of compound 24 retained an optimal distance and orientation toward the P-loop cysteine of FGFR1, facilitating efficient Michael addition. After covalent conjugation, compound 24 interacted with the hinge region and precisely matched the unique FGFR1 conformation. Its robust antitumor activity was validated in cellular, CDX, and PDX models by suppressing FGFR1-dependent tumor growth, providing a novel strategy for subtype-selective FGFR1 inhibitor development.

item.title: Design and Biological Evaluation of a Potent Dual PARP and BRD4 Inhibitor for Tumor Therapy via Disrupting HRR and BRD4-cJUN-CCL2 Axis
item.description:
Abstract
Inducing homologous recombination repair (HRR) deficiency is an attractive strategy to expand the therapeutic scope of PARP inhibitors. Since BRD4 inhibition impairs HRR function and sensitizes cancer cells to PARP inhibition, we designed and synthesized a series of dual PARP/BRD4 inhibitors. Structure−activity relationship studies identified D6 as a potent dual inhibitor with low nanomolar inhibitory activities against PARP1 and BRD4. D6 exhibited potent antiproliferative activity in MDA-MB-231 and KP4 cells and induced cell cycle arrest, apoptosis, and inhibition of colony formation and metastasis-associated phenotypes. Mechanistically, D6 suppressed the BRD4-cJUN-CCL2 signaling axis, reducing macrophage recruitment and macrophage-mediated cancer cell invasion. In an MDA-MB-231 xenograft model, D6 inhibited tumor growth without obvious toxicity. These findings support D6 as a promising dual PARP/BRD4 inhibitor for cancer therapy.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Antifibrotic Evaluation of Silicon-Incorporated Alkyl Hydrazide Analogs of Tubastatin A: HDAC3 Selective Inhibitor for Ameliorating Liver Fibrosis
item.description:
Abstract
Liver fibrosis remains a significant therapeutic challenge, with limited effective treatments and few clinically viable HDAC inhibitors despite their antifibrotic potential. Here, we report the design of silicon-incorporated alkyl hydrazide analogs of tubastatin-A to develop selective HDAC3 inhibitors via cap and zinc-binding motif optimization. These compounds were evaluated for HDAC-selectivity and antifibrotic activity in TGF-β-induced HSC-LX2 and HHSEC models, where 6b exhibited potent and selective HDAC3 inhibition (IC50-22 nM) with respect to HDAC5, HDAC6, HDAC8 along with robust antifibrotic activity, supported by molecular docking. ADMET studies indicated a favourable pharmacokinetic profile, permeability, microsomal stability, and a promising safety profile. Further validation in a CCl4-induced hepatic-fibrosis model, 6b demonstrated significant in-vivo efficacy by reducing AST/ALT levels, fibrotic marker expression and improving histopathology, outperforming tubastatin-A and nintedanib. Mechanistically, 6b significantly inhibited TGF-β/Smad signaling, likely through modulation of histone-acetylation patterns. Collectively, these findings identify 6b as a promising lead candidate for hepatic fibrosis.

item.title: Synthesis and Structure−Activity Relationship (SAR) of Hydroxypyridone-3-carboxamides against Orthopoxviruses
item.description:
Abstract
We have previously identified hydroxypyridone-3-carboxamide 4a as a potent antiviral hit against vaccinia virus (VACV) and monkeypox virus (MPXV), albeit with extremely low solubility. Herein, we have conducted antiviral structure−activity relationship (SAR)-directed and solubility-driven synthesis of a total of 57 analogs. In the primary VACV reporter assay, many analogs demonstrated nanomolar to sub-micromolar antiviral potency without significant cytotoxicity, with analog 4m showing 10-fold improved potency. Plaque assays against VACV and MPXV confirmed the strong antiviral activities. We also discovered that amide N-methylation drastically enhanced solubility via disrupting an intramolecular H-bond. Specifically, we identified an N-methylated analog (4f) with >1000-fold improved solubility while retaining potency (EC50 = 0.69 μM). In addition, compound 4f exhibited dose−response potency against MPXV in the plaque assay and highly favorable ADME properties. Overall, our current work characterizes 4f as a strong antiviral lead and solidifies amide N-methylation as a viable approach toward further lead development.

item.title: Discovery of Novel Pyridine-Dihydropyrrolo[3,4- b ]Pyrrolidone Derivatives as Orally Active PIM Kinase Inhibitors for the Treatment of Acute Myeloid Leukemia
item.description:
Abstract
PIM kinases are promising therapeutic targets for acute myeloid leukemia (AML). Merging PIM447 with C28 via molecular hybridization, we successfully designed and synthesized a series of novel pyridine-dihydropyrrolo [3,4-b]pyrrolidone derivatives. Among them, compound 50 exhibited potent inhibitory activity against PIM-1/2/3 (IC50 = 6.71/15.14/10.10 nM, respectively) and significant antiproliferative activity against MV4-11 cells (IC50 = 0.21 μM). Mechanistic studies demonstrated that 50 dose-dependently inhibited substrate phosphorylation (e.g., BAD), thereby inducing PARP cleavage, apoptosis, and G2/M arrest. It possesses favorable drug-like properties and high oral bioavailability. Kinase profiling against 217 kinases showed good PIM selectivity. In an MV4-11 xenograft model, oral administration of 50 at 50 mg/kg once daily achieved 84.7% tumor growth inhibition without significant toxicity, and platelet toxicity was lower than C28. Overall, compound 50 is a potent, orally bioavailable PIM kinase inhibitor with a favorable safety profile that warrants further systematic evaluation in AML models with diverse genetic backgrounds.

item.title: Synthesis, Spectroscopic, Computational, and PDT Investigations of a Series of Cationic Meso -(3-pyridyl)-indolylstyryl-BODIPYs
item.description:
Abstract
Boron dipyrromethene (BODIPY) dyes bearing a meso-(3-pyridyl) moiety have found multiple applications, such as pH and metal ion sensors, fluorescence probes, and as sensitizers for phototherapy. A series of 3-mono- and 3,5-di-indolylstyryl-BODIPYs bearing a meso-(3-pyridyl) group and different 2,6-substituents (H, Cl, Br, I) was synthesized and their properties investigated. The extension of π-conjugation via the indolylstyryl groups produced bathochromic shifts in the absorption and emission spectra of up to 200 nm, while the introduction of the heavy 2,6-iodo groups induced the highest in vitro and in vivo phototoxicity. In a comparison study with Photofrin, mono-indolylstyryl-BODIPY 4a cat was found to be a potent photosensitizer (IC50 = 11 μM at 3 J/cm2; under the same conditions Photofrin’s IC50 = 24 μM) in HT-29 cells. In mice bearing HT-29 xenograft tumors, BODIPY 4a cat shows similar PDT efficacy as Photofrin and is the most promising photosensitizer among the new series of meso-(3-pyridyl)-BODIPYs.

item.title: Imidazo[1,2- a ]pyrazine Derivatives as Dual A 2A /A 2B Adenosine Receptor Antagonists Enhancing Anti-PD-1 Antibody Therapy in Colorectal Cancer
item.description:
Abstract
Adenosine signaling through A2A and A2B adenosine receptors (ARs) suppresses antitumor immunity and promotes tumor progression, limiting immune checkpoint blockade in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (CRC). Here, we identified imidazo[1,2-a]pyrazine-urea derivatives as a new chemotype of dual hA2A/hA2B AR antagonists. SAR studies revealed that 3-iodination of the core scaffold enhanced receptor affinity and functional antagonism, with 5p emerging as a representative lead. MD simulations showed that 5p can be accommodated in the orthosteric pockets of both AR subtypes through distinct binding modes, with the 3-iodo substituent occupying adjacent subpockets. Representative compounds inhibited adenosine-induced CREB phosphorylation, restored Th1 cytokine production, and increased CD4+ and CD8+ T cell infiltration. In CD73-high CRC models, 5p suppressed tumor growth and potentiated anti-PD-1 efficacy. These findings support dual A2A/A2B AR antagonism as a strategy to reprogram the adenosine-rich tumor microenvironment and improve CRC immunotherapy.

item.title: Discovery of Novel Orally Bioavailable STING Inhibitors with 4,5,6,7-Tetrahydropyrazolo[1,5- a ]pyrazine Moiety for STING-Mediated Inflammatory Disorders
item.description:
Abstract
The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)-stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway plays a pivotal role in host defense against pathogenic microbes and tumors. However, aberrant activation of this pathway is tightly associated with a wide spectrum of inflammatory and autoimmune disorders, positioning STING inhibition as a promising therapeutic strategy. In this study, we designed and synthesized a series of novel 4,5,6,7-tetrahydropyrazolo[1,5-a]pyrazine derivatives as STING inhibitors. Compound 37 displayed potent STING inhibitory activity and favorable in vivo pharmacokinetic properties and safety. Further studies revealed that 37 blocks STING palmitoylation, thereby suppressing downstream signaling pathway activation. Oral administration of 37 exhibited significant anti-inflammatory effects in 10-carboxymethyl-9-acridanone (CMA)-challenged mice, Trex1−/− mice and cisplatin-induced acute kidney injury (AKI) mice. Collectively, compound 37 represents a novel orally bioavailable STING inhibitor with therapeutic potential against STING-driven inflammatory and autoimmune diseases.

item.title: Structure-Based Design of 2-(Pyridone)Indoles as Antagonists of the Toll-Like Receptors TLR7 and TLR8 for the Treatment of Autoimmune Disorders
item.description:
Abstract
Toll-like receptors 7 and 8 (TLR7/8) are innate immune sensors whose activation by endogenous RNA ligands is a hallmark of chronic autoimmune disorders, notably cutaneous and systemic lupus. We present the structure-based design and optimization of 2-(pyridin-2(1H)-one)indoles as potent dual TLR7/8 antagonists with properties improved over our prior series, including increased permeability, reduced ion channel activity, and reduced volume of distribution at steady state (Vss). Initial pyridone leads displayed unexpected anti-proliferative activity in a panel of immune cell lines; optimization against an identified off-target BRD4 liability, hypothesized to drive this effect, delivered potent antagonists devoid of BRD4 binding and of anti-proliferative activity. These compounds potently inhibited TLR7/8-mediated IL-6 production in human whole blood, with 9a giving IC50 values of 9.4 and 1.3 nM against TLR7 and TLR8, respectively. This orally bioavailable lead dose-dependently suppressed TLR7-mediated IL-6 and IFNα release in a mouse pharmacodynamic model.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation of 1 H -Pyrrolo[3,2- c ]quinolines as Potent and Selective Antitubulin Agents Active against Drug-Resistant Cell Lines
item.description:
Abstract
A library of 1H-pyrrolo[3,2-c]quinolines (PQs) was synthesized, and SAR analysis identified compounds with low-nanomolar potency in CCRF-CEM cells (IC50 = 13−18 nM) and selectivity indices > 1000-fold over BJ fibroblasts. The most active derivatives retained activity against daunorubicin-resistant and paclitaxel-resistant sublines, indicating limited cross-resistance, and compounds 4, 14, and 17 showed efflux ratios < 2 in MDR1-MDCK and Caco-2 assays. Colchicine-site engagement was supported by various assays and docking/MD simulations. ADME profiling showed high chemical and plasma stability, plasma protein binding, and moderate-to-high microsomal clearance. After i.p. dosing in CD-1 mice at 12 mg/kg, compound 17 reached a maximum plasma concentration (Cmax) of 879.9 ng/mL (2.73 μM) at tmax = 15 min, with a 103 min half-life and limited brain penetration. In zebrafish embryos, 17 induced concentration-dependent developmental abnormalities (LC50 = 198 nM at 96 hpf), consistent with antimitotic activity but pointing to a narrow therapeutic window.

item.title: Design, Synthesis, and Biological Evaluation of Novel Benzimidazole Derivatives as Dual PI3K/HDAC8 Inhibitors with Potent Anti-Cervical Cancer Activity In Vivo
item.description:
Abstract
The dual inhibition of phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase (PI3K) and histone deacetylase 8 (HDAC8) has emerged as a promising strategy for cervical cancer (CC) therapy. We synthesized 34 novel benzimidazole derivatives and evaluated their anti-CC cell line proliferation. The compound 50 exhibited equivalent antiproliferative effect to cisplatin (Pt) in CC cell lines SiHa, Ca Ski, and HeLa, especially in HeLa cells with an IC50 value at 1.42 ± 0.50 μM (Pt 1.70 ± 0.28 μM). Further assessment in the HeLa cell xenograft mouse model, the intraperitoneal medium- (30 mg/kg) and high-dose group (60 mg/kg) and and intragastric high-dose group (100 mg/kg) exhibited antitumor efficacy no less than that of Pt (i.p. 5 mg/kg) but much more safe during the experiment period. Mechanism studies demonstrated that 50 could inhibit the PI3K/Akt pathway and HDAC8 expression and function. These findings prove that the PI3K/HDAC8 dual inhibition may be an efficient way in cervical cancer treatment and compound 50 deserved for further development.

item.title: Electrophile-First Screening Identifies Covalent Aminothiazole Scaffold Inhibitors for Ubiquitin-Conjugating Enzyme UBE2D2
item.description:
Abstract
UBE2 family of E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes occupy central positions in multiple ubiquitination pathways and have been implicated in cancers, motivating efforts to develop chemical probes to interrogate their functions. In this study, we identified XY54 as a covalent modifier of UBE2D2 that engages both C85 and C111 by using an electrophile-first screening approach coupled with X-ray crystallography. Structure-guided structure−activity relationship optimization of XY54 yielded XY54-24, in which modifications of the amide and ester groups of XY54 selectively abolished its binding to C111 while enhancing affinity for C85. XY54-24 inhibited UBE2D2 enzymatic activity in vitro and suppressed the proliferation of A549 lung cancer cells. Collectively, this study identifies covalent aminothiazole scaffold inhibitors for targeting UBE2D2 and provides a structural foundation for further development of selective UBE2D2 chemical probes.

item.title: Discovery of Threonine Tyrosine Kinase (TTK) Degraders Utilizing an Electrophilic Monomethyl Fumarate Handle
item.description:
Abstract
Threonine tyrosine kinase (TTK), a core component of the spindle assembly checkpoint, plays an essential role in mitosis, and its inhibition has emerged as a promising therapeutic strategy for human cancers. We previously reported multiple approaches to target TTK, including reversible inhibitors, covalent inhibitors, and PROTAC degraders. In this study, we advance these efforts by developing a novel monovalent degrader of TTK. The representative compound, 26, generated by appending an electrophilic monomethyl fumarate handle to a TTK inhibitor, effectively induced TTK degradation and demonstrated superior antiproliferative activity across diverse cancer cell lines. Mechanistic investigations suggested that compound 26 primarily engages RNF126 and stabilizes its association with TTK, thereby inducing TTK ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Collectively, this work provides the first example of a TTK molecular glue-like degrader and introduces a new electrophilic handle for the rational design of degraders with reduced nonspecific cytotoxicity.

item.title: Discovery of Pyrazolo[1,5- a ]-1,3,5-Triazine Derivatives as Potent, Highly Selective and Orally Available Macrocyclic CDK7 Inhibitors
item.description:
Abstract
Cyclin-dependent kinase 7 (CDK7) is a promising cancer therapeutic target due to its dual role in cell cycle progression and gene transcription. However, current CDK7 inhibitors generally exhibit poor kinase selectivity. Herein, we performed in-depth structural optimization on a 17-membered macrocyclic scaffold, and identified compound I-23, which potently inhibits CDK7 with an IC50 value of 3 nM and exhibits exceptional CDK7 selectivity with no significant off-target activity across 416 kinases. I-23 also potently inhibits cell proliferation across a panel of tumor cell lines, induces cell cycle arrest and transcriptional suppression, and downregulates oncoprotein c-Myc, particularly in triple-negative breast cancer cells. Importantly, I-23 shows favorable oral bioavailability (up to 28%) with linear pharmacokinetics. Collectively, this work provides a highly selective and orally bioavailable macrocyclic CDK7 inhibitor, which can serve as a valuable chemical tool for dissecting CDK7 biological functions and a promising lead compound for CDK7-based anticancer drug discovery.

item.title: Discovery of YKS-34 , a Highly Selective PDE4B Inhibitor for the Treatment of Idiopathic Pulmonary Fibrosis
item.description:
Abstract
Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF) remains a progressive and fatal lung disease with a substantial unmet need for safe and effective therapies. Highly selective inhibition of phosphodiesterase 4B (PDE4B) represents a promising therapeutic strategy for IPF while avoiding nausea and vomiting associated with PDE4D inhibition. However, achieving pronounced subtype selectivity remains particularly challenging; notably, the only approved PDE4B-preferential inhibitor, nerandomilast, exhibits only approximately 9-fold selectivity for PDE4B over PDE4D. Herein, we report the identification of YKS-34, a potent PDE4B inhibitor (IC50 = 1.71 nM) exhibiting >1000-fold selectivity over PDE4A, PDE4C, and PDE4D. YKS-34 effectively suppressed TGF-β-induced fibroblast activation and LPS-induced TNF-α release in vitro. In vivo, YKS-34 showed favorable pharmacokinetic properties, lung tissue accumulation, and reduced emetic potential at tested conditions while dose-dependently improving pulmonary dysfunction and fibrotic remodeling in a bleomycin-induced IPF mouse model. Consequently, YKS-34 emerges as a highly promising, next-generation candidate for the treatment of IPF.

item.title: Design and Synthesis of Novel, Non-ATP-Competitive MKK3 Modulators as Suppressors of TNF-α Production for the Treatment of Ulcerative Colitis
item.description:
Abstract
Although TNF-α is a clinically validated target for Ulcerative colitis (UC), therapy is dominated by injectable biologics, with no oral small-molecule inhibitors approved. Traditional ATP-competitive p38 inhibitors designed to regulate TNF-α have failed in clinical trials due to poor kinome selectivity. As the primary upstream activator of p38, MKK3 is considered a promising alternative target, but the development of small molecules remains limited, with a notable absence of non-ATP-competitive modulators. Herein, we report a series of compounds targeting the non-ATP-competitive pocket of MKK3 to suppress TNF-α production. Among them, (R)-48 was identified as a lead candidate, demonstrating robust suppression of TNF-α (IC50: 0.038 μM), high oral bioavailability (62.6%), clear dose-dependent efficacy and strong PK/PD relationships in mouse UC models. Particularly, HDX-MS suggested (R)-48 probably binds to a distal allosteric site on MKK3, precluding TAK1-mediated activation. Altogether, (R)-48 emerges as a promising oral small-molecule therapeutic candidate for the treatment of UC.

item.title: Development and Preclinical Evaluation of Six-Transmembrane Epithelial Antigen of Prostate 2 Targeted PET Probes: A Case of Drug Repurposing Based on Molecular Docking
item.description:
Abstract
Six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of prostate 2 (STEAP2) is overexpressed in prostate cancer, yet no STEAP2-targeted imaging probes exist. Using molecular docking, we screened triptorelin and leuprorelin by radioiodine labeling and identified triptorelin as a high-affinity, selective ligand. To enhance in vivo stability and pharmacokinetics, triptorelin underwent acetylation, PEG extension, and 4-iodophenylbutyric acid conjugation, yielding five DOTA-conjugated analogs radiolabeled with 68Ga. In 22Rv1 xenografts, 68Ga-Trip-5 exhibited moderate but specific tumor uptake (SUVmax 1.8) with favorable tumor-to-background contrast. In vivo stability, biodistribution, pharmacokinetics, and human radiation dosimetry (effective dose 0.00345 mSv/MBq) demonstrated favorable safety. Autoradiography on human prostate cancer specimens showed probe accumulation correlating with endogenous STEAP2 expression. This represents the first STEAP2-targeted PET probe developed via molecular docking-guided drug repurposing. Cellular, biochemical, and imaging data provide supportive evidence of STEAP2-mediated targeting. Preclinical performance supports clinical translation of 68Ga-Trip-5, with definitive target validation

item.title: Synthesis and In Vitro/In Vivo Stability Evaluation of Various Radioiodinated Tyrosine Derivatives
item.description:
Abstract
Radioiodinated drugs face limited application due to severe in vivo deiodination. In this study, nine tyrosine derivatives were synthesized and evaluated to develop stable radioiodinated prosthetic groups to reduce deiodination. Biodistribution results revealed that replacing phenolic hydroxyl and amino groups with methoxy and acetamide groups enhanced stability. Compound 131I-8 exhibited the highest stability, with a maximum thyroid uptake of 1.13 ± 0.12 %ID (approximately one-20th of 131I-Tyr). It’s high stability was explained by in vitro stability experiments and molecular docking. A new PSMA-targeted radioiodinated drug, [125/131I]IMPA, was synthesized to verify whether compound 8 remained stable after conjugation with drugs. It exhibited a lower thyroid uptake of only 0.19 ± 0.03 %ID, approximately 100-fold lower than that of the control compound [131I]ITPA, which has a tyrosine moiety as the radioiodination site.
